system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-06-12 18:08:00 to 2179-06-19 12:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Crohn’s disease, status post subtotal colectomy and ileosigmoid anastomosis, was admitted with a one-week history of worsening right-sided abdominal pain, increased watery bowel movements up to 100 per day, and bright red blood per rectum. He had recently started Tysabri therapy. CT imaging showed worsening wall thickening and hyperemia in the sigmoid colon, consistent with active inflammatory bowel disease, with no evidence of obstruction or infection. Stool studies and CMV testing were negative. He was initially treated with antibiotics, which were discontinued after negative cultures. Due to persistent symptoms, a steroid burst with prednisone was initiated in consultation with his specialist, leading to improvement in bowel frequency and pain. His back pain was evaluated with MRI, which showed stable degenerative disc disease without new neurological compromise; he was managed with Percocet and tizanidine. He improved clinically, was transitioned to oral medications, and discharged home on a prednisone taper, continued Tysabri and B12 injections, and pain regimen with follow-up planned with GI and spine services.
problems: Displacement of lumbar intervertebral disc without myelopathy
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ male with Crohn's and abdominal pain.

STUDY:  Supine and upright abdominal radiographs.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  There is no free intraperitoneal air.  There are no dilated loops
of bowel or air-fluid levels.  There is no pneumatosis.

IMPRESSION:  No obstruction or free intraperitoneal air.

HISTORY:  ___ male with abdominal pain.

STUDY:  Upright chest radiograph.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  The cardiomediastinal and hilar contours are normal.  The lungs are
clear.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  The osseous structures
are intact.  There is no subdiaphragmatic free air.

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary process and no subdiaphragmatic free
air.

MEDICAL HISTORY:  ___ man with Crohn's disease and nephrolithiasis
presenting with colicky right flank pain.  To evaluate for nephrolithiasis or
flareup in Crohn's.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen  dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT were acquired in axial images involving the
abdomen and the pelvis before and after administration of 130 mL of Optiray
contrast.  Oral contrast was also administered for the study.  Coronal and
sagittal reformats were performed at 5-mm slice thickness.

FINDINGS:  

Few, focal scattered areas of illdefined subpleural infiltrates are visualized
in bilateral lung bases.  No evidence of pericardial or pleural effusion
noted.

The liver, spleen, pancreas, bilateral adrenals and kidneys show normal CT
anatomy without any focal or diffuse lesions.  Normal pattern of enhancement
is also noted in the viscera.  The stomach is normal in caliber.

The patient is noted to be status post colonic resection with ileosigmoid
anastomosis.  In comparison to the previous study, the area of ileosigmoid
anastomosis and length of colonic resection could not be precisely localised
on this study. Please refer surgical notes for the same. A segment of bowel
loop at the expected rectosigmoid junction demonstrates thickened, enhancing
wall measuring about 6 cm atleast in length(4A;71. A prominent nodular
thickening is seen on the medial wall of this loop which may represent a
inflammatory intramural phlegmon.  There is  stranding of fat around the
abnormal-appearing loop noted.  The immediate small bowel loops proximal to
this segment appears to be mildly dilated. A few enhancing periaortic lymph
nodes are noted with no significant mesenteric lymphadenopathy.

There is no free air within the abdomen noted.

The bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles and ureters appear normal.  No
evidence of renal or ureteral calculi noted.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  There are no acute fractures, dislocation, lytic or
sclerotic lesions suspicious for abnormality is noted.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No evidence of nephrolithiasis or ureteric calculi bilaterally.
2.  Status post colectomy with ileosigmoid anastomosis.  Inflammation
involving a bowel segment at the recto-sigmoid junction with a focal
intramural phlegmon is noted which demonstrates interval progression. Mildly
dilated bowel immediately proximal to this abnormal appearing segment is seen.
However, there is no evidence of free fluid,abscess, fistula or  free air
seen.

INDICATION:  History of nephrolithiasis, severe flank pain, assess for
hydronephrosis, obstruction or passing stone.

TECHNIQUE:  Renal ultrasound.

COMPARISONS:  CTU ___.

FINDINGS:  Right kidney measures 10.3 cm.  The left kidney measures 10.8 cm. 
There are two echogenic foci within the right kidney without definite
shadowing but with ringing down, which are likely vascular in nature.  There
is no definite evidence for stone, hydronephrosis, or mass.  The bladder is
normal in appearance.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence for stones, hydronephrosis, or mass.

LUMBAR SPINE MRI WITHOUT CONTRAST, ___

INDICATION:  ___ man with Crohn's disease and history of
nephrolithiasis who presents with acute right flank/back pain and left groin
pain radiating to the testicle.

COMPARISON:  Lumbar spine MRI dated ___, at which point the
patient had severe lower back pain radiating down the left side.

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal T1- and T2-weighted images of the lumbar spine were
obtained, with axial T2-weighted images from L2-3 through L5-S1.

FINDINGS:  Vertebral body height and alignment are normal.  Bone marrow signal
is within normal limits.

At T11-12, there is a disc bulge minimally indenting the ventral thecal sac,
but not contacting the distal spinal cord, unchanged since the previous study.
The conus medullaris is normal in signal intensity, terminating at T12-L1.

The L1-2 through the L3-4 levels are unremarkable.

At L4-5, there is a mild disc bulge and facet arthropathy, left worse than
right, without significant spinal canal or neural foraminal narrowing.  There
is fluid in the left facet joint.  These findings are unchanged.

At L5-S1, there is an asymmetric disc bulge, slightly larger on the left,
which causes mild right and moderate left neural foraminal narrowing,
unchanged since the prior study.

No signal abnormalities are identified in the imaged retroperitoneal soft
tissues.

IMPRESSION:  Unchanged mild degenerative disease.  Moderate left and mild
right neural foraminal narrowing at L5-S1.

INDICATION:  History of inflammatory bowel disease.  Right leg swelling.

TECHNIQUE:  Right lower extremity ultrasound.

COMPARISON:  None available.

FINDINGS:  Grayscale and Doppler sonograms of the right common femoral,
superficial femoral and popliteal veins were performed.  There is normal
compressibility, flow and augmentation.  Calf veins were not visualized.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of deep venous thrombosis.

RIGHT ANKLE ON ___

HISTORY:  Inflammatory bowel disease.  Right ankle swelling, evaluate for
fracture or effusion.

IMPRESSION:
Three views of the right ankle show moderate soft tissue swelling on the
medial side, just inferior to the malleolus, with no fractures, derangement,
foreign body or gas in the soft tissue or good evidence for joint effusion on
the lateral view.  I see no joint erosion or narrowing.  Deformity of the
posterior malleolus of the tibia could be post-traumatic from remote injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having some pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it's this sharp pain in my upper right abdomen. It comes and goes, but it never really goes away. It’s different from my usual left-side pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how long has this been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About two days now. I thought maybe it was a blockage because it’s so intense and on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any vomiting, fever, or blood in your stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no vomiting or fever. And no blood. But my stools have been less frequent—only about four times a day instead of my usual 14. They’re more formed too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually a good sign. We’ll run some tests to see what’s going on. You’re on prednisone, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 5 mg daily. I was on 10 mg a week ago, but I tapered down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve already done a basic X-ray of your abdomen and chest. No signs of blockage or free air, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not based on the X-ray. But we’re going to do a CT scan with contrast to get a better look at your bowel and rule out kidney stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had Crohn’s flares before, but this one feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan is back. Good news—no kidney stones or abscess. But there is increased inflammation at your ileosigmoid anastomosis, worse than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s a flare-up? But why the right-side pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The inflammation is near the rectosigmoid junction, which might be referring pain to the right. The bowel just before that area is also a bit dilated, which could contribute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious? No abscess or perforation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, no free fluid, abscess, or perforation. That’s very good. We’re going to start you on IV steroids to calm the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on Tysabri—could that be helping or making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tysabri is meant to help control Crohn’s. You’ve had three infusions—your team thinks it’s still appropriate to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back clean—no infection. Stool tests also negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely Crohn’s, not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, looks like active inflammation from Crohn’s. We’re stopping antibiotics and focusing on anti-inflammatory treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is up—15.7. But that’s likely from the steroids, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in this case. Steroids often raise white blood cells. You’re not febrile, and cultures are negative, so we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been having some back and flank pain. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. You have tenderness on the right flank. We’ll do a kidney ultrasound and an MRI of your spine to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The kidney ultrasound is back—no stones, no hydronephrosis. Your kidneys look structurally normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling an MRI of your lumbar spine to see if there’s any nerve involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: MRI results are in. Your spine shows mild degenerative changes, same as before. No new disc herniation or nerve compression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain isn’t from my back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not directly. The changes are stable. Your pain might be referred from the bowel inflammation or muscular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also noticed some swelling in my right ankle. Should we check that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ll get an X-ray and ultrasound to rule out clot or joint issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ankle X-ray shows soft tissue swelling but no fracture. Ultrasound shows no DVT. Likely related to inflammation from Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So all these pains are connected to my Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. The abdominal inflammation is the main driver. The other symptoms—ankle, back, flank—could be extraintestinal manifestations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on IV steroids. When can I switch to pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll switch you to oral prednisone tomorrow. You’ll take 40 mg daily, then taper over weeks with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enemas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, hydrocortisone foam twice daily for 10 days. It helps target the inflammation right at the anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—now 8.6. You’re afebrile and eating well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Prednisone 40 mg daily, tapering with your GI doctor. Pantoprazole, B12 tablets instead of shots, and tizanidine for muscle tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oxycodone for breakthrough pain—only for a few days. Then stop. We’re limiting it due to your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I don’t want to rely on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re making good progress. Follow up with your GI and primary doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Keep taking your meds as prescribed, especially don’t stop prednisone suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Taper slowly with my GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. And call if you develop fever, severe pain, or bloody stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for helping me through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of refractory ileocolonic Crohn’s disease, status post subtotal colectomy and ileosigmoid anastomosis, was admitted with a two-day history of severe colicky right upper abdominal pain, nausea, and reduced bowel frequency. He had recently tapered prednisone from 10 mg to 5 mg daily and was on Tysabri therapy. Initial imaging showed no obstruction or free air. A CT scan revealed worsening inflammation at the rectosigmoid junction with a focal intramural phlegmon and mild proximal bowel dilation, but no abscess or perforation. Workup for nephrolithiasis, infection, and DVT was negative. MRI of the lumbar spine showed stable degenerative changes. He was treated with IV solumedrol and hydrocortisone enemas, then transitioned to oral prednisone. His pain improved, white count normalized, and he was discharged home on a prednisone taper, rectal steroids, and continued Tysabri with follow-up planned with gastroenterology.
